analysis.one_liner: Requires a binding ethics code, gift rules, and conflict-based recusal for Supreme Court justices.
analysis.headline: The bill has 94 cosponsors, all Democrats, and has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since the day it was introduced in May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write enforceable ethics rules for the nine Supreme Court justices into federal law. It requires the Court to adopt a code of conduct, sets gift disclosure and gift-acceptance rules matching those for members of Congress, forces justices off cases where a party gave them money or gifts, and creates a process for litigants to challenge a justice's refusal to step aside. It would also require groups filing 'friend of the court' briefs to reveal their funders. As of now, it has gone no further than a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary litigants and the public at large. Anyone whose case reaches the Supreme Court gains a rule that a justice must step aside if a party or its affiliates gave the justice income, gifts, or reimbursements in the six years before the case, or spent money supporting the justice's appointment. The public gains searchable public access to the Court's ethics rules, published explanations whenever a justice is disqualified, and mandatory disclosure of who funds amicus briefs, which today can be filed by undisclosed interests to sway the Court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Litigants and public trust in courts

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to adopt a formal code of conduct for justices, with public notice and comment, within 180 days of enactment.
Directs the Court's Counselor to set gift-acceptance and disclosure rules for justices and their law clerks at least as strict as the rules that bind members of the House and Senate.

Adds new automatic disqualification grounds: a justice must recuse where a party or its affiliate lobbied or spent substantial funds supporting the justice's nomination or appointment, or where a party or affiliate gave the justice, their spouse, or minor child income, gifts, or reimbursements within six years of the case.

Creates a procedure for a party to formally seek a justice's disqualification, with the motion decided by the other eight justices when it targets a Supreme Court justice, and requires the justices to publish explanations of disqualification decisions.

Requires anyone filing an amicus brief to disclose the people who prepared it and any funder who gave over $100,000 or 3% of the amicus's annual revenue, with an annual government audit of compliance.
Requires parties and amici to disclose gifts, income, lobbying contacts, or spending connected to any justice's nomination, confirmation, or appointment.

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices, who would face written rules, mandatory disclosure, and mandatory recusal for the first time; wealthy litigants and well-funded organizations that currently file anonymous amicus briefs or have favorable relationships with justices, who would lose that discretion; and the judiciary generally, which would absorb administrative costs for complaint panels, audits, and studies.

drawbacks.text: The complaint and review machinery runs largely inside the federal judiciary itself: the Supreme Court writes its own code, and the panel that investigates complaints against a justice is drawn from other federal judges, so skeptics argue the bill creates self-policing rather than true external enforcement.

Recusal at the Supreme Court is decided by the other eight justices under the bill, which means recusal fights could become political battles and a determined justice could still sit on a case if eight peers decline to disqualify them.

The bill layers new disclosure duties on parties, law firms, and amicus filers, which adds compliance costs and paperwork for routine litigation, and the amicus funding thresholds could sweep in trade associations and nonprofits for ordinary reporting burdens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and concrete: for the first time, justices would face written conduct rules, gift limits equal to those on members of Congress, and automatic disqualification when money connects them to a party before them. The main cost is administrative burden on courts and filers, plus the design compromise that the judiciary polices itself. Those drawbacks are modest next to the current situation, in which the justices are the only federal judges with no enforceable ethics code and litigants have no formal way to challenge a conflict of interest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and nothing has happened since: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal, and Transparency Act of 2025 on May 20, 2025, joined by 28 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction, which is the only action it has received.
The bill attracted 94 cosponsors in total, every one of them a Democrat, with no Republican support.
The House Judiciary Committee has held no hearing or markup on the bill and the House has not voted on it; the bill remains pending with the Congress still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete. The justices, big litigants, and undisclosed amicus funders keep the current arrangement under which the Supreme Court sets its own ethics rules and recusal is at each justice's sole discretion, and a bill with broad Democratic support has made no progress toward a vote.

for.name: Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 94 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, making the bill one of the more broadly supported House ethics bills of the session, though entirely from one party.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controls the House floor calendar and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or floor action on the bill since its referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee majority
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held no markup on the bill in the months since referral, leaving it without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors are Democrats and the original 28 sponsors were all Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican majority that controls the House calendar has taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill ends the justices' status as the only federal judges without an enforceable ethics code, imposing gift limits, disclosure, and mandatory recusal for money connections to litigants. Individual justices and interests tied to them lose discretion they have today.

industries.industry: Wealthy litigants and parties before the Court
industries.note: Organizations and individuals with financial relationships to justices would face automatic recusal and mandatory disclosure of gifts and lobbying on justices' appointments. Their interest in keeping those channels undisclosed runs against the public's interest in impartial courts.

industries.industry: Amicus brief filers (trade groups, advocacy organizations, corporate interests)
industries.note: Today anyone can file a friend-of-the-court brief without revealing funding. The bill requires funders above $100,000 or 3% of revenue to be named, with an annual audit, removing a low-visibility channel of influence over the Court.

The bill requires disclosure of lobbying contacts made to support a justice's appointment and bars judges from cases where a party lobbied for their appointment, and requires parties to disclose gifts and income their lawyers gave to justices. Compliance burdens fall on firms, but the disclosure targets are the justices' conflicts.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsor, a Republican-held House, and no committee activity five months after referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing, markup, or floor vote this Congress. The most likely path is that it sits in the Judiciary Committee and expires at the end of the session; a parallel path would be a Senate-introduced companion bill, but the House would still need to act.
